lines: Rust on a sword is just neglect learning to speak.
Trouble always finds villages. <bold>Best be ready.</bold>
A blade tells the truth about its owner sooner or later.
Ready is not the same as eager. A village should know the difference.
Keeping an edge honest is mostly knowing when to stop grinding.
An unready guard is just confidence standing in the wrong place.
Most days, I am at the grindstone, trying to keep balance and edges from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think weapon work is simple until one bad edge proves otherwise.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good hammer more than a loud promise. The hammer has less to prove.
A blade is only honest in hands that know restraint.
Sharp work begins before the edge touches the stone.
Weapons are promises of trouble. I prefer them well made and rarely needed.
Balance matters because panic already pulls hard enough.
A nick in a blade tells you where fear met metal.
The grindstone rewards patience and punishes showing off.
A village needs defense, but it should never start enjoying the need.
Good steel is calm until someone asks too much of it.
I judge a weapon by how safely it rests, not only how fiercely it swings.
The best edge is the one that ends danger quickly and goes quiet again.
A heavy weapon teaches truth through wrists and shoulders.
I have seen more harm from careless hands than from dull blades.
Smithing weapons means respecting the peace they might fail to protect.
A straight blade still needs a straight reason.
Steel remembers every bad angle.

The edge is healthy. Do not ruin it with careless strikes.
Keep the blade dry and it should serve you for a long time.
No cracks, no loose parts, and no bad surprises.
Someone has been taking proper care of this weapon.
The wear is even. That usually means the wielder knows what they are doing.
I would trust this in a fight after one quick cleaning.
The point is sound and the handle still sits straight.
Nothing here needs the forge yet.
A light pass on the stone is all this needs.
Do not overwork the edge just because the weapon is in good shape.
This has seen action and come through it cleanly.
The fittings sound solid when I test them.
Good steel lasts when its owner respects it.
Bring it back when the grip starts to move, not after it comes apart.

There are enough nicks here to change how the blade moves.
It can still work, but I would not carry it into a long fight.
The edge is tired and the fittings show strain.
Repair it now while the work is simple.
This weapon has been used hard without enough time at the bench.
The wear near the grip concerns me more than the scratches.
A few more heavy strikes could turn a small repair into a broken weapon.
The balance is starting to pull away from the hand.
I can clean up the edge, but the handle needs attention too.
Serviceable is not the same as dependable.
Do not let the shine distract you from the loose fitting.
The damage is manageable if you stop using it for now.
I would replace that binding before it fails under pressure.
This has one more fight in it, but that is not a promise I like making.
Bring it to the forge before the next serious trip.
You caught the wear in time. Let us keep it that way.

Put it away. The edge is ready to fail.
That crack will spread on the next hard strike.
The grip is loose enough to hurt the person holding it.
I would not trust this to cut rope, let alone face trouble.
One more fight could leave you holding pieces.
This needs a forge, not another target.
The damage has gone past ordinary wear.
Do not swing it again until the fittings are replaced.
The balance is wrong because the weapon is coming apart.
I can repair this, but only if you stop using it now.
A desperate weapon makes a desperate fight worse.
The edge has chips deep enough to catch and break.
You waited too long, but there may still be enough steel to save.
Set it down carefully. I do not trust that handle.
This is the kind of damage that fails without warning.
Carry a spare until I finish the repair.
A broken weapon always chooses the worst moment. Do not give it the chance.
Remember when I followed you and you hit me? Poor weapon discipline. Worse friendship.
When did the plan change from a journey into an ambush?
Did you expect me to trust you after striking from that close?
Why lead me down the road if you meant to turn on me?
Was the attack planned, or did you lose control?
Do you understand why I watch your hands now?
What did you think would happen after we made it home?
Did the quiet after the blow bother you at all?
Why should I believe your directions after that?
Would you have done the same if I had kept my weapon drawn?
Did you notice I was watching the path instead of you?
How long had you been waiting for my guard to drop?
Was there ever an honest destination, or was that part a lie too?
Do you know what betrayal does to a person who trusted your lead?
What would you call a guide who becomes the danger?
Did you expect an apology to erase the walk home?
Why did you wait until we were away from the village?
Can you give me one reason to follow you again?
Do you remember the exact moment I stopped trusting you?
If we speak about that road, are you finally going to tell the truth?
That boat trip had one good quality. No one was swinging steel in it.
Did you check the hull before we pushed away from shore?
Why did the current take us so far off the route?
Was my weapon safer in its sheath or back at the village?
Did you know how little room there would be to move?
What was knocking under the hull when the water got deep?
Would a lighter blade have made any difference in that boat?
How were you steering while every small movement rocked us?
Did you see the village disappear behind us?
What would you do if something attacked from the water?
Was that landing where you meant to take us?
Did you choose the boat because it was safer than the road?
How close did we come to turning over when the current caught us?
Would you trust the same boat a second time?
Why did nobody tell me that sitting still could be hard work?
Did you keep track of the shore, or were you following the current?
What part of that trip worried you most?
If we crossed again, where would you tell me to put the weapon?
Did the ground keep moving for you after we stepped out?
Can we agree to inspect the boat together next time?
A weapon is not courage. It is just steel waiting to learn who holds it.
Blades should be sharp enough to end danger, not start arguments.
The best sword in the village is the one that never needs a story.
A weapon tells me plenty before anyone swings it.
I check the grip before the edge. A loose handle ruins good steel.
Wear near the guard shows how a weapon has really been used.
A polished blade can still be badly balanced.
The reason someone drew a weapon matters as much as the weapon itself.
Good repairs disappear into the balance. Bad ones announce themselves.
A disciplined hand knows when to leave steel sheathed.
The edge gets attention, but the fittings keep it safe.
I trust honest wear more than a mirror shine.
A heavy blade punishes a careless grip.
Every nick has a story, and most are not flattering.
Inspect the whole weapon before you praise it.
Steel only behaves as well as the person carrying it.
A sound weapon should feel calm in the hand.
The grindstone can fix an edge. It cannot fix bad judgment.
A weapon should protect the village without ruling it.
If the balance feels wrong, believe your wrist.
